data.title: Wall Street ends higher as battered AI stocks gain in volatile week
data.description:
NEW YORK - Wall Street’s main indexes ended higher on Nov 27 and posted weekly gains as investors returned from the Thanksgiving holiday and flocked to hard-hit AI-linked shares.

US stocks have swung sharply this week, with Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO and Anthropic’s brief fall below its initial public offering price adding to volatility across the AI trade.

Investors have alternated between bargain-hunting after a steep selloff and fretting over soaring AI costs, heavy borrowing and doubts about companies’ returns on investment.

“The market is so oversold that a bounce was inevitable,” said Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group.

Chipmakers that investors battered this month recovered ground, with Micron and Marvell gaining 7.6% and 7.3% respectively. The broader chip gauge also climbed 4.7%. Nvidia, after remaining weak for most of the session, ended 0.8% higher.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to 50,774.94, the S&P 500 gained 114.71 points, or 1.60%, to 7,297.49 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 543.70 points, or 2.31%, to 24,129.50.

AI beneficiaries, including data-storage firm Sandisk , surged almost 16%, while optical-products maker Lumentum and server maker Dell also gained sharply.

AI hyperscalers – tech companies that run large data centers – also rose, with Amazon.com, Microsoft, Meta Platforms and Oracle posting gains. Tesla surged 5%.

“There is a bounce in technology which started Monday, continued Wednesday with an intraday reversal and now continues today. So much fast money has delevered out of tech that this could have persistence next week as they are forced to chase back in,” said Andrew Slimmon, senior portfolio manager at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

Weekly gains

For the week, the S&P 500 gained 5.6%, the Nasdaq rose 6.68%, and the Dow climbed 5.46%. The S&P 500 weekly gain was the index’s biggest since April 2025.

The S&P 500 bank index rose 1.6%, fuelled by JPMorgan Chase’s almost 2% gain.

The market’s gains have done little to erase November’s losses. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq are on track for their worst November since 2008, pressured by concerns over tougher AI regulation following the Democrats’ US midterm election victory and expectations that monetary policy will remain restrictive.

Traders are almost fully pricing in a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December after data this week showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter and inflation accelerated further in October.

Gold and silver miners rallied as precious-metal prices recovered from a bruising few sessions. Newmont gained 5.4%, while the Global X Silver Miners ETF also advanced.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals slid 5.2% after the US Food and Drug Administration extended its review of the company’s kidney-disease drug by up to three months.

US equity markets were open for a half-day session on Nov 27, following the Thanksgiving holiday on Nov 26.

Volume on US exchanges was 10.97 billion shares.

Advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.25-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 55 new highs and 73 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 3,677 stocks rose and 1,135 fell as advancing issues outnumbered decliners by a 3.24-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 12 new 52-week highs and no new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 53 new highs and 96 new lows. REUTERS

data.title: Airline Norse Atlantic’s Norwegian operating unit declares bankruptcy
data.description:
OSLO – Budget carrier Norse Atlantic said on Nov 27 it would file a petition for bankruptcy for its main Norwegian operating unit and was halting ticket sales and cancelling all flights, becoming the latest airline casualty of fuel-cost spikes stemming from the war in Iran.

Norse is the second European airline to enter bankruptcy proceedings in 2026 after Latvia’s airBaltic, highlighting the toll of the Iran war on carriers that entered the crisis without fuel hedges as jet fuel prices surged.

The company said it had not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs, with the board deciding to file a bankruptcy petition on Nov 27 with the Agder District Court in Norway for its operating subsidiary.

“The Board, management and advisers of the listed entity Norse Atlantic ASA and the UK subsidiary are working to find a solution for the remaining part of the business to continue operations,” Norse’s chief executive officer Eivind Roald said in a statement.

Roald held a virtual meeting with Norse’s employees at 1pm GMT, according to Norwegian media.

The company had 1,071 employees as at June 30, its latest quarterly filing showed.

The airline is advising passengers against going to the airport as it has stopped flying, adding that customers could submit a claim for a refund in the insolvency process, though that would not guarantee payment, while customer service is no longer available.

“This is a very hard day for the pilots and their families, and for all other Norse employees. Our thoughts are also with the passengers whose journeys are now cancelled,” the board of the Norse Atlantic Pilots Association told Reuters in a statement.

Aircraft owners terminate leases

Norse Atlantic said on Nov 25 that its financial situation was “critical”. The following day, it said it had suspended all flights and that the board could file for bankruptcy unless it urgently secured funding.

Earlier on Nov 27, Norse said its lessors had terminated their leasing contracts for all 12 aircraft in the carrier’s fleet, demanding that the planes be handed back, a claim contested by the company.

Norse in 2021 signed long-term leases for nine Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft from Ireland-based AerCap Holdings and six Dreamliners from Singapore-based BOC Aviation. It later returned three of the planes to AerCap.

“The company contests the validity of the termination notices,” Norse said in a statement.

The AerCap leases were due to run for about 12 years for each aircraft, while the BOC contracts were due to run for 16 years, according to Norse’s latest annual report.

“Although they are contesting the notices, it sounds pretty decisive. Unless successful in this, they will not be able to resume operations,” said aviation analyst John Strickland.

BOC declined to comment when contacted by Reuters. AerCap did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Worst aviation crisis since pandemic

Founded in 2021 by entrepreneur Bjorn Tore Larsen, Norse sought to revive budget transatlantic flights after Norwegian Air abandoned long-haul operations during the pandemic.

But as a pure long-haul player, Norse Atlantic lacked a “feeder” service from regional connections, which industry analysts early on said could hamper efforts to fill the start-up carrier’s transatlantic flights.

The airline later diversified into charter and aircraft leasing services as it struggled to generate profits from scheduled flights alone.

The global aviation industry is suffering its worst crisis since the Covid-19 pandemic as the US-Iran conflict, which began at the end of February, disrupts operations, drives up fuel prices, and sends airlines’ costs skyrocketing. REUTERS

data.title: Sri Lanka credit rating upgraded
data.description:
COLOMBO – An international agency upgraded Sri Lanka’s credit rating to B- on Nov 27, its first change in more than a year, as the island nation continues its economic recovery.

S&P Global Ratings said it reflected efforts to strengthen fiscal and external buffers since the 2022 crisis, when the country defaulted on US$46 billion (S$59.31 billion) in external debt.

It raised Sri Lanka’s foreign currency and local currency sovereign credit ratings from CCC+ to B-, with a stable outlook.

In September 2025, S&P removed Sri Lanka from “Selective Default” status, assigning it a junk rating of CCC+.

Sri Lanka secured a US$2.9 billion International Monetary Fund (IMF) bailout after the crisis, which is expected to be fully disbursed by March.

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake unveiled his 2027 budget in November, projecting US$2.08 billion in foreign funding.

The IMF forecasts that Sri Lanka’s growth will slow to 4% in 2026 from 5% in 2025, as higher global energy costs weigh on the economy.

It has said Sri Lanka has proved “remarkably resilient to successive shocks” but has also warned of risks from the Middle East war, global trade uncertainty and the El Nino climate phenomenon. AFP

data.title: Real incomes in S’pore rise but at slower pace in 2026, with smaller gains for lower-wage workers
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Workers in Singapore saw their incomes grow in 2026 but at a slower pace, after taking higher inflation into account.

Real median income of full-time employed residents rose by 2.2% in 2026, down from 4.1% in 2025.

For workers at the 20th percentile of the income distribution, real income growth slowed to 1.3%, from 3.6% the year before.

The nominal median monthly income of full-time resident workers – before accounting for inflation – rose to $6,021 in 2026, up from $5,775 in 2025. This is the first time the figure has exceeded $6,000. For 20th-percentile earners, it grew by 3.4% to $3,270, from $3,164 in 2025.

The figures were released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report.

The figures are preliminary as full-year inflation data for 2026 is not yet available.

MOM said the slower growth partly reflected more cautious wage increases by firms and higher inflation. Consumer prices are projected to rise by around 2% in 2026, compared with 0.9% in 2025.

The ministry said that despite the slower gains for lower-wage workers in 2026, their incomes have grown faster than those at the median over the recent five- and 10-year periods.

It added that they will continue to be supported by progressive wage measures.

Permanent jobs remain the norm

MOM noted that employment quality remained broadly stable even with softening manpower demand and continued external uncertainty.

Employees accounted for 88.2% of employed residents in 2026.

Among resident employees, 91% held permanent jobs, edging up from 90.8% in 2025.

The share of employees on fixed-term contracts remained stable at 7.1%, while casual or on-call employment declined further to 2%.

Over the decade, there was a shift among fixed-term contract employees towards longer contracts of at least a year, the ministry said.

Unemployment rates

While Singapore’s unemployment rate stayed low overall, there were signs of greater pressure on workers in non-professional roles.

The unemployment rate among non-professionals, managers, executives and technicians (non-PMETs) rose from 2.8% in 2025 to 3.5% in 2026, returning to levels seen in 2023 and 2024.

In contrast, unemployment among PMETs remained broadly stable at 2.7%.

The long-term unemployment rate, which measures the proportion of workers who have been unemployed for at least 25 weeks, edged up to 0.7% for both groups.

Among non-PMETs, the increase was driven by workers aged 50 and above.

Residents in their 50s recorded the highest incidence of retrenchment, rising from 2.4 to 3.6 per 1,000 employees between the second quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026.

Their six-month re-entry rate was also consistently below the overall average.

MOM said at a briefing on Nov 27 that the increase in the unemployment rate for non-PMETs can be attributed to difficulties faced by older non-PMETs in securing employment.

The hiring conditions in certain sectors also softened. The long-term unemployment rate in sectors more exposed to the global economy, such as manufacturing and wholesale trade, rose from 0.7% in 2025 to a five-year high of 0.9% in 2026.

Overqualification

With the Singapore workforce being increasingly educated, the share of resident workers in PMET jobs rose to 65.2%.

But the overqualification rate has declined for the third consecutive year from 19.4% in 2025 to 18.7% in 2026, while the involuntary overqualification rate remained low at 1.6%. The latter suggests that a few workers were in jobs below their qualifications because they could not find suitable alternatives, MOM said.

The profiles of the voluntarily and involuntarily overqualified were “broadly similar”. Of the tertiary-educated, 47.7% worked as associate professionals, while 50.8% worked as technicians. This reflects younger workers taking up entry-level jobs to gain experience for higher-skilled jobs, MOM said.

Labour under-utilisation, which refers to the unemployed, under-employed and discouraged workers, remained low in 2026.

The number of discouraged workers, which refers to people who gave up on their job search, remained low at 7,100, or 0.3% of the resident labour force.

There has been a slight dip in the proportion of part-time workers who are willing and available to do additional work, with the time-related under-employment rate declining from 1.9% in 2025 to 1.7% in 2026.

Ageing workforce

Singapore’s labour force participation rate eased further for the fifth consecutive year since 2021, but remains largely stable despite its ageing population, hovering at 67.9% in 2025 and 67.8% in 2026.

Higher participation among women has helped to offset some of the pressures of an ageing population.

The labour force participation rate rose across most five-year age groups, with larger increases among seniors.

Coupled with seniors’ growing share in the population, the proportion of residents aged 60 years and above in the labour force rose from 13.1% in 2016 to 19.5% in 2026.

Singapore’s labour force participation rate also ranked among the world’s highest – placing seventh across the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development’s member countries – ahead of countries such as Switzerland, Estonia and Australia, MOM noted.

The findings in the advance labour force report were drawn from the annual Comprehensive Labour Force Survey, which covers a representative sample of 33,000 households. A total of 27,292 households responded to the survey conducted from March to July.

data.title: Fewer people in S’pore changed jobs in 2026, but most who did earned more: MOM
data.description:
SINGAPORE – Fewer workers in Singapore have been changing jobs as hiring slows and more seek job stability, even though those who have switched employers have been more likely to get a higher pay.

About two-thirds, or 65.6%, of full-time resident employees aged 25 to 64 who changed jobs saw their incomes rise after accounting for inflation, with most of these gains amounting to at least 5%.

The figures were released by the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) on Nov 27 in its annual labour force advance report.

The proportion of employed residents who changed jobs in the past year fell to 5.7% in 2026, extending the gradual downtrend from its peak in 2022.

The decline in job switching was most pronounced among younger residents aged below 30, particularly those aged 15 to 24. Younger workers who stayed in their jobs cited job stability as the most common reason for staying.

Meanwhile, older workers aged 50 and above were least likely to change jobs, with around half of older job stayers holding on to their current jobs for at least a decade.

MOM also tracked the longer-term income outcomes of workers who changed jobs, and found that they were more likely to enjoy real income gains than those who did not, director of MOM’s manpower research and statistics department Ang Boon Heng noted at a media briefing on Nov 27.

Job switchers were more likely than job stayers to see real income gains, with about 67% of them receiving higher incomes from 2025 to 2026, compared with around 61% who stayed in their jobs.

The gap widens when looking at a five-year period from 2021 to 2026. For example, the older cohort who changed jobs in 2021 saw their incomes rise over a longer period following the job switch.

More than nine in 10 job switches over the past year were voluntary rather than due to retrenchments, said MOM.

Income outcomes were weaker in a small segment of workers who changed jobs involuntarily. Around 58% enjoyed income gains in their new job relative to their previous job, lower than the 67% recorded among voluntary job switchers.

While the majority of both groups saw higher incomes when they switched jobs, the ministry noted that involuntary job switchers were less likely to surpass earnings made in their old jobs.

Many job switchers moved across industries or occupations. Residents who changed industries typically remained in or moved into industries with above-average productivity, such as wholesale trade and financial and insurance services, while those who changed occupations commonly moved between PMET (professionals, managers, executives and technicians) jobs.

These cross-sector and cross-occupation transitions show how transferable skills and experience can support workers to navigate labour market changes, said MOM.

Job mobility continued to slow across most sectors, including professional services and financial and insurance services, partly reflecting softer hiring and business restructuring.

But the information and communications sector showed an exception, with the share of employed residents who changed jobs edging up from 8.1% in 2025 to 8.7% in 2026. MOM said the increase indicates ongoing workforce reallocation efforts and changing skill needs as firms adapt to technological developments.

data.title: Global economy risks hangover as growth over-reliant on AI boom: India chief economic adviser
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The global economy may be posting strong headline growth, but much of it perches atop the pinnacle of artificial intelligence – a bubble that may already have begun to deflate.

Speaking at the Asia Future Summit on Nov 27, the chief economic adviser to the Indian government, Anantha Nageswaran, cautioned against taking post-pandemic economic resilience for granted.

“There is a sense of fragility attached to these growth numbers because they have been somewhat disproportionately reliant on one particular sector and all the capital expenditure associated with that,” he said.

“(Growth) has not necessarily percolated down to vast segments of the population... and there are also financial system vulnerabilities that are built up,” he added, stressing the need to prepare for a potential post-bubble fallout.

He made the remarks during a panel discussion at SPH Media’s annual thought leadership conference, which returned for its fifth edition in 2026.

For the first time, it was jointly presented by the media organisation’s key news titles: The Straits Times, The Business Times, Lianhe Zaobao, Berita Harian and Tamil Murasu.

OCBC Bank is the presenting sponsor, with Marina Bay Sands as the official venue partner and Amazon Web Services as the official cloud partner.

Nageswaran was part of a panel discussion, moderated by BT senior correspondent Ben Paul, titled “Are we headed for a global crisis? How will Asia’s economies respond?”

The other three panellists were: Akmal Nasir, Malaysia’s Minister of Economy; Guo Shan, partner at Hutong Research; and Loh Boon Chye, Singapore Exchange (SGX) group chief executive.

Asked about AI’s long-term impacts on productivity, Nageswaran replied that the real question was not just whether such gains accrue, but also to whom they do.

“If the productivity gains accrue predominantly to owners of capital – but not to owners of labour – and if there is widespread labour displacement that happens... then it will not be an enduring productivity gain,” he said.

Pointing to the risks of financial destabilisation arising from the web of interwoven financing that characterises today’s AI sector, he added that a more important question was how to calculate productivity gains that are adjusted for the potential risks unleashed by AI models.

Diversify risks, not just portfolios

The risks of overconcentration were also highlighted by SGX’s Loh, who cautioned that a diversified portfolio did not necessarily translate into diversified risks.

Loh framed the AI debate around three questions:

Acknowledging that the US remains the biggest market and an enduring one, he added that opportunities abound around Asia as well.

But while opportunity can create economic value, it does not necessarily lead to investment returns, he cautioned, noting that risk could increase with continued geographical concentration.

Still, he maintained that he was not seeing signs that investors were oblivious to their overall AI exposure or the concentration risks in their portfolios.

Of chips and China

Turning to China, Guo said that the latest developments surrounding US restrictions on AI chips could accelerate an adjustment in the sector, bringing forward the expected demand-supply rebalancing to 2027, ahead of the previously anticipated 2028.

The restrictions could affect up to 30% of the demand in the chip industry, she said, as many of China’s hyperscalers rely on overseas data centres.

This would also prompt China to accelerate its domestic production, she added.

Guo does not expect Beijing to respond with another round of economic stimulus, noting that China’s economy is still on track to meet Beijing’s annual growth targets.

There is no urgency for any stimulus; rather, the central bank has been focusing on fiscal prevention, she continued.

Guo also pointed to signs that Beijing is seeking to play a more active role in stabilising the global economy, including by addressing concerns over China’s large trade surplus.

She noted that China has publicly pledged to pursue what it calls “international circulation” – a shift she said is arguably the first time China is seriously looking at its international role and how it can be a more responsible player in the global economy.

“Beijing sees that the global market has to be (integrated). We have to stabilise the supply chain so that everybody will enjoy a better business environment.”

She said that this would involve three things for China: importing more, maintaining exports and encouraging its firms to expand overseas. She added that this approach is reminiscent of Japan’s efforts to rebalance its trade in the 1980s.

One common factor that would drive these three developments is the renminbi’s appreciation, added Guo.

“I’m looking at the renminbi to stabilise in the next year but, in the long term – we’re talking towards 2035 – we’re probably looking at the renminbi to appreciate by 40%,” she said.

Malaysia turns to value creation

Malaysia, meanwhile, is seeking to capture more value from the AI boom by moving up the semiconductor supply chain, said Akmal.

While the country has traditionally been known for chip testing and packaging, it is now looking to develop higher-value capabilities further up the chain.

The government is also becoming more selective about data centre investments, with closer scrutiny of their energy and water use.

The economic spillover of such investments should extend beyond real estate and construction, and into helping build up Malaysia’s AI capabilities and those of the wider region, he added.

The Malaysian minister concluded: “We cannot build our economic strength on geopolitical rivalries... we want to be part of the solution in this very challenging world (and) definitely we need to preserve our reputation.”

By contrast, India has had relatively little exposure to the market-led AI boom, said Nageswaran, pointing to the absence of listed Indian companies among the major beneficiaries of the investment surge.

He was responding to an audience question on India’s limited presence in the AI discourse despite its established software industry.

But this could also leave the country less exposed to a potential correction, he noted.

“It also means that, because India was not part of the party, it would not be part of the hangover,” he said, contending that the party was “more or less over”.

THE BUSINESS TIMES

data.title: ‘Not about certification for certification’s sake’: What HR credentials can offer firms and workers
data.description:
SINGAPORE – After spending more than 20 years in operations and industry development, Wilson Tan moved into a regional human resource role at his company, Stolz Engineering, in 2024.

The senior manager of people, culture and organisational capability described the transition as one that left him with “a quiet dose of impostor syndrome”.

He said gaining certification from the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) helped him bring more structure to work he had previously approached through operational instinct. He added that his employer gave him the flexibility to study alongside carrying out his regional responsibilities and apply what he learnt at work.

When handling workplace changes, Tan now uses IHRP’s Body of Competencies as a guide. This national competency framework defines the skills, knowledge and mindsets HR professionals need to deliver strong employee experiences and sustainable business value.

During the roll-out of a company-wide enterprise resources planning system and career conversion programmes, he said he listened to employees’ concerns and explained how the changes could reduce repetitive work and support their growth.

“I learnt to step back, see challenges through an objective lens, and ‘think like a marketer’ by actively selling the ‘why’ to secure genuine buy-in rather than forcing compliance.”

By July 1, 2028, organisations with more than 200 employees must have at least one suitable HR professional certified at IHRP Certified Professional level or higher.

An equivalent qualification may also be accepted, subject to IHRP’s bridging requirements.

Requirement covers 2,000 organisations

The requirement covers about 2,000 organisations, including 300 with at least 1,000 employees and 40 with at least 5,000, according to an earlier parliamentary reply by Acting Manpower Minister Jasmin Lau.

Together, the organisations employ more than 45% of Singapore’s total workforce. About 45% already have at least one IHRP-certified HR professional.

Lau also said the 200-employee threshold was chosen as a practical starting point, focusing on companies with the scale and means to take the lead on certification.

IHRP has seen more e-mail inquiries and participation in certification application clinics since the requirement was announced in September, its chief executive Aslam Sardar said.

He added that the certification requirement is a minimum baseline and encouraged employers to develop capabilities across their HR teams. The number of professionals a company should certify would depend on its size, business needs and workforce complexity, he said.

IHRP encourages employers to identify candidates early and offers preparation materials and assessment tutorials. Training partners, including the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), also run preparatory programmes.

SNEF chief executive Hao Shuo said employers should set aside time for candidates to prepare, particularly to refresh their knowledge of Singapore’s labour laws. Some companies may need to balance preparation with manpower constraints and operational demands, he said.

What the 2028 HR certification requirement means

Eligible Singapore citizens and permanent residents can receive a one-time $100 subsidy between Oct 1, 2026 and June 30, 2028, bringing the IHRP Certified Professional certification fee to $163.50, inclusive of goods and services tax.

Eligible candidates can also use SkillsFuture Credit, while employers will be able to tap a redesigned SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit, with further details to be announced.

The certification is valid for three years.

The July 2028 deadline gives employers time to prepare, said a Ministry of Manpower spokesperson, who encouraged them to start early and make use of available support.

Carol Yap, director of HR and administration at Safran Aerosystems Services Asia, believes certification gives her company assurance that its HR professionals have the knowledge and competencies to fulfil roles effectively.

Certified as an IHRP senior professional, she said her biggest hurdle was taking the first step to register for certification. “Having spent more than 20 years in the HR profession, I found myself questioning whether I really needed another certification.”

She added: “I don’t think obtaining the certification necessarily changes the way I practise HR. After all, the experience and knowledge gained over more than 20 years in the profession have shaped the way I approach HR matters today.”

Nonetheless, revisiting HR case studies allowed her to refresh and reinforce her understanding of HR practices and employment legislation, she said, adding that the preparation journey was “a valuable learning experience”.

NTUC assistant secretary-general Patrick Tay stressed that the 2028 requirement does not require every HR professional to be certified, “so individuals should not feel pressured to pursue certification regardless of their circumstances”.

“Ultimately, this is not about certification for certification’s sake,” he said. “It is about strengthening HR capabilities so that companies are better equipped to make fair and responsible workforce decisions, and workers can have greater confidence in how these decisions are made”.

data.title: Thakral Corp aims to ride the waves of a revitalised stock market with spin-off listing: CEO
data.description:
SINGAPORE – The local equities market has been given a boost in recent years, thanks to Singapore’s efforts to inject liquidity into the market and draw more interest among investors.

One company that sees more potential in the local market is conglomerate Thakral Corporation, which is eyeing a spin-off of its lifestyle business to be listed on the Singapore Exchange (SGX), which would unlock value for the company.

Thakral has already seen two of its investee companies successfully list on separate stock exchanges in recent years.

Next in line is its lifestyle business, which distributes L’Oreal beauty and fragrance products in Greater China and Japan, Nespresso in India, and DJI drone products across South Asia.

The lifestyle business is one of the group’s fastest-growing segments. Quarterly revenue for the lifestyle segment rose 40% year on year to $137 million for the third quarter that ended Sept 30, up from 34% growth in the first half of 2026.

Thakral chief executive Inderbethal Singh Thakral told The Straits Times that he had no immediate plans to propose a listing, but the boost the SGX has received in recent years made him reconsider.

“We were looking at maybe two or three years later. Then we saw all these changes coming about with the Equity Market Development Programme (EQDP) and what we saw in some of the other companies around us,” said Bethal, as he is more popularly known.

The EQDP initiative was launched in February 2025 and was part of measures to revitalise the sluggish local equities market. Since then, the Monetary Authority of Singapore has allocated $5.4 billion across 14 appointed asset managers through multiple batches to increase market liquidity.

“I like where the SGX is going, especially with the focus on small and medium enterprises,” Bethal said.

Thakral has also felt some trickle-down effects of the stock market initiatives, including the Value Unlock programme by SGX to help small and mid-cap companies realise their value through shareholder engagement and other measures.

Bethal said Thakral is “still in the hopeful stage”. The company has seen some increase in trading volumes, but there have also been periods of dips, perhaps because of geopolitical uncertainty, he said.

As part of unlocking value, Thakral is also engaging more with shareholders by holding more meetings with them throughout the year and reaching out through investor relations and corporate communications. This is vital as shareholders might find it challenging to understand the different businesses of the conglomerate, Bethal said.

Thakral is also participating in the Elevate side of SGX’s Value Unlock programme, which provides a grant for companies to take on deeper shareholder engagement, through targeted support and connecting companies with consultants to sharpen market positioning.

Bethal said Thakral’s strategy of spinning off businesses is one way it creates value for the company. Listing the lifestyle business in particular would also help shareholders better understand the overall conglomerate, as they can see the value of the separate businesses and add up the sum total of the various entities.

Spinning off will also help his successor to deal with the different businesses under Thakral, Bethal said.

“For me, I have been juggling all these balls for over 50 years. I don’t even feel that these are different businesses for me,” he said. “But spinning off can help to streamline the company for the next person who comes and takes my place.”

Bethal, 66, has been with Thakral since 1975 and became its CEO in 2016.

Singapore-headquartered Thakral, which was listed on the SGX mainboard in 1995, has a real estate business that includes commercial buildings in Japan and a mixed-use healthcare project in India. It also has a stake in Australia-listed GemLife, which develops and operates resort-style residential communities exclusively for people aged 50 and above in Australia.

Thakral also launched and grew the China business of The Beauty Tech Group, a UK-based company that produces and sells clinically inspired at-home beauty devices, through a joint venture.

On Nov 19, Thakral said it was selling its minority stake in the business, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange. The sale comprised 6.7 million shares at £5.05 per share – 86% above the business’ initial public listing price of £2.71 in October 2025.

Meanwhile, its lifestyle business saw growing revenue from South Asia in the third quarter, where Thakral is the authorised distributor for DJI, a Chinese manufacturer of drones, handheld cameras and gimbals.

Demand has benefited from the rapid growth of India’s creator economy, particularly the increasing popularity of short-form video and video content creation, Thakral said on Nov 12.

The lifestyle segment also saw more revenue from its Greater China network including Hong Kong and Macau, through its distribution of fragrance brands such as Maison Margiela Fragrance, Miu Miu, Viktor & Rolf, Ralph Lauren Fragrance, Atelier Cologne, Mugler and Yue Sai.

Thakral is also growing its fragrance presence in Japan through pop-up stores opening in Tokyo and Osaka.

It expects the lifestyle segment to exceed 25% growth for the 2026 full financial year.

If the lifestyle business spin-off is successful, Thakral will retain other businesses like its drone component manufacturing in India, which is separate from its DJI distribution business.

Bethal sees that the outlook for drone manufacturing is bright, with demand coming from agriculture companies and enterprises, and not just individual content creators.

Offering drones-as-a-service might also be an opportunity, he said.

“In five years’ time, we might have the same conversation on spinning it off,” he said. “But for now, the drones segment is still at a start-up stage.”

data.title: Danantara unit’s management of RGE’s revoked Indonesia forest concession is temporary, reports say
data.description:
JAKARTA – A newly established unit of Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara will temporarily manage the forestry concession seized from Singapore-based conglomerate Royal Golden Eagle (RGE), local media reports cited a Danantara executive as saying.

The Indonesian government last week revoked forest usage permits covering 338,536ha that had been granted to Riau Andalan Pulp and Paper (RAPP), a unit of RGE, in Riau province, citing fires and other violations.

Management of the area was transferred to Garuda Adidaya Nusantara, a newly established Danantara subsidiary, this week.

“The Forestry Ministry appointed us as a temporary manager. It’s not an acquisition,” Danantara chief operating officer Dony Oskaria said, according to media reports late on Nov 26.

He said the company would manage the concession during the legal process to ensure there was no disruption to operations and no impact on RAPP employees or nearby communities.

Danantara and BP BUMN, the state company regulator also headed by Dony, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

An RAPP spokesperson has said the company believes it has operated in compliance with all applicable regulatory requirements in managing its concessions.
